channel.title: Joel Winkelman
channel.description: Joel Winkelman is Assistant Professor of Government and Public Policy at Hamilton College.

item.title: Starting to sift the fragments
item.description:
I spent the last two weeks processing archival documents, and I thought it might be helpful to me to try and think out loud about what I’m doing.

First of all, I’m noticing how wild it is that ordinary academics at mid-century had secretaries who typed their correspondence. The carbon copies on the onionskin paper with the initials of the secretaries below the signature; the “dictated but not signed” notice; the few handwritten notes when someone was writing from vacation are all remarkable windows into the lifeworld of the period. It’s an occupation whose history I feel I should know more about. It makes me want to identify these people if possible through the books whose typing they surely did. Or perhaps the typists of books were different administrative support staff.

The second thing I notice is how the densest correspondence is the most professional and business-like. The thickest folders are the ones with many letters produced by secretaries, meaning things the people whose archives I’m now sifting through did not feel it worth their time to write themselves. For letters they wrote themselves did not produce carbon copies. Or at least, I’m assuming this to be the case. In this way, the archive is rather less revealing than I want it to be. Or, rather, it is less personally revealing. It still reveals directions of thought, especially amid the ferment of an ongoing project. Letters show colleagues reaching out to one another to share ideas. But the letters typed by secretaries rarely give a glimpse behind the professional mask.

A better way to say it, however, is that what is revealed is always interpretive and inferential. In the two archives I have recently visited, folders tell a story that the principal wants posterity to hear. Thomas Szasz wants people like me to know that he was a friend to the civil rights movement in the early 1960s. Harold Lasswell wants people like me to know that he proposed forming an agency that would centralize intelligence functions at the same time that “Wild Bill” Donovan was. People want to be remembered in a certain way and for specific actions, arguments made, or positions taken relative to the history that they (at some point) realized they were living through.

What I wonder is whether and how to use this as evidence, and, if so, what kinds of questions it can help to answer. When Thomas Szasz and his mentor Therese Benedek share a letter about a paper he gave at the Institute for Psychoanalysis in Chicago about his use of “game” language to describe the psychoanalytic situation between patient and therapist, what is that evidence of? How should that be weighed against his published bibliography? And when the two sources (published and unpublished) diverge, how do I make sense of that divergence?

And what about the substance of some of the letters? Szasz is remembered today, if he is remembered at all, as a crackpot libertarian, a bit of a provocateur who lent his name, likeness, and reputation to a number of dubious causes in search of fame. Yet, the archives are full of letters from individuals seeking his help in securing their release from involuntary psychiatric commitment, or restitution after their hard-won release. Some are women whose husbands or fathers had them committed involuntarily after some slight, fight, or rebellion. Some are civil rights protestors who are sent to psychiatric hospitals after their arrest at marches. Some are former military men who are held for reasons they don’t understand, but suspect an effort to prevent them from sharing their involvement in legally suspect activities.1 And some letters are from people who did have an acute experience of (what we would call) mental illness who are now finding it impossible to secure their own release. The letters are tender, and Szasz’s response is cordial, graceful, and often sorrowful. He simply can’t do very much for most of these people unless they secure some legal representation. And yet, he’s also the same person who serves as an expert witness for the prosecution in cases whose lurid details suggest the acts of someone who could not possibly know right from wrong, whose explanations of their deeds are so detached from any consensus reality that ascribing criminal responsibility seems absurd at best, and cruel at worst. And here is Szasz, flying to California and collecting a handsome fee for helping to prevent an insanity defense.

The last thing I’ll say is that I’m noticing how hard it is to make sense of anything. A life seen so close is always complicated. It makes me feel tempered in my judgments. After all, were my life subjected to such scrutiny, who knows what interpretations others would develop. Moreover, I have photographed so many letters and pieces of correspondence. Then, I write up my summary of what each letter says, trying to make sense of a conversation that I am usually tuning in to midstream. In most cases, I’m having to trust that something of use will emerge because its immediate relevance is not clear. In some cases, it’s one or two sentences for every dozen letters. For others, it’s one or two letters for every dozen folders. Either way, the hit rate is small. I’m finding that it’s best not to think too hard about the low efficiency of the work and just be so thankful that I have the time and space to be doing it. The suspension of judgment is good practice, and so is resisting the feeling that every bit of my attention needs to have its value maximized.

Footnotes

  1. These letters are interesting because of their soft-pedaled paranoia.↩︎

item.title: Psychiatry in social science
item.description:
I’m on a train coming back from a week of work in the archives and the APSA annual meeting. The particular collection I was looking at was the papers of Harold Lasswell, an important 20th-century political scientist. I don’t think many political scientists are “important” in the way Lasswell was, and I don’t think Lasswell’s importance has been fully appreciated, despite several awards named in his honor. And, after this visit, I don’t think historians of American institutions fully appreciate how much Lasswell helped to shape the post-war U.S. national security state (but that’s the subject for a conference paper, not an entry in my public notebook).

The reason Lasswell first caught my eye, actually, was an attack on him by Thomas Szasz in Psychiatric Justice. I had known a little bit about Lasswell because two students had written nice undergraduate theses on him with me. One student’s thesis, in particular, got me very curious about Lasswell and his apparent use of Freudian concepts. I had known him primarily as the author of a pithy aphorism about politics being “who gets what, when, how.” I knew he had made some contributions to the rise of behavioralism in the discipline, and had also written a canonical piece of early international relations theory about some concept he termed “the garrison state.” I had, at that point, probably never consciously read him.

Of course, when Lasswell’s Freudianism came to my attention via a student paper, I presumed that the student was, if not mistaken, exaggerating or stretching the claim. Although it was an honors thesis, undergraduates tend toward hyperbole. And then I saw Thomas Szasz write about Harold Lasswell suggesting that a corps of “policy scientists” deploy around the country to conduct social psychiatry to assist citizens in their healthy adjustment to the psychic demands of democratic life. That certainly got my attention and sent me to the primary texts.

I found when I read Lasswell’s Psychopathology and Politics that my student had not been exaggerating. And when I read Lasswell’s Power and Personality, I found that neither had Szasz. At first, I thought these projects were more connected than they have turned out to be. There’s no indication in Lasswell’s papers that he had any sustained or deep engagement with Thomas Szasz. Any debate was one-sided, and I think Szasz was partly picking a fight to try and get social scientists to pay attention to him (“rage-baiting,” or “engagement farming” in the parlance of our times) and there is no debate that could be staged between them as an intellectual set piece à la the Dewey-Lippmann debate or the Du Bois-Washington debate. But they do mark two poles of the intellectual current that carried psychiatry as an intellectual project from an interpretivist activity to a positivist one.

What I find most interesting about Lasswell was his willingness to use the tools of psychiatry for the purposes of social adjustment. I am interested in how Lasswell thought the state should use psychiatric knowledge for its own national interest. And I am interested in how Lasswell justified it, if he did at all. After my visit to the archives, I’m increasingly thinking that he didn’t. After all, he wrote in his 1936 book Politics: Who Gets What, When, How that thinking might be great for “locating oneself as an object among objects in the march of time,” but it was also useful as a way to “discover ways and means of gaining goals.” I think his work on behalf of the state was in part a test of this hypothesis about the role of thinking.

item.title: Enter Thomas Szasz
item.description:
In addition to Eric Berne, the current psychiatry project also considers Thomas Szasz, an important figure in the related anti-psychiatry and deinstitutionalization movements. The paper I’m currently working on as I write this update attempts to work out their relationship to one another and their relative importance to some of the intellectual currents of the time, notably the interdisciplinary formation we know as “game theory.” I’m writing this down to help clarify for myself what got me hooked on these two unusual figures.

I noticed the connection between them when I was seriously reading Games People Play. As I mentioned before, the book is dated and problematic in all kinds of ways. Nevertheless, I found it compelling as an intellectual document. One of the reasons that I found it so interesting is because my most important work at the time was a civic project that involved facilitating weekly group therapy with youth in jail who were facing adult charges. One of my co-facilitators was an older psychiatric social worker whose day job was in a state mental hospital. I’ve written about this elsewhere, if anyone is curious. It was a weird chapter of life. Knowing a little bit about Berne’s “transactional analysis” gave me at least one way of understanding the work we were doing, however dated his concepts.

But apart from its use in this specific and unusual collaboration, I have to admit that I found some of the “game analysis” verified in daily experience. My professional life kept showing me examples of Berne’s “Why Don’t You — Yes But” (YDYB) game. It had a bit of Myers-Briggs or Enneagram to it, the same parlor-game kind of appeal. Berne, however, didn’t see it as a parlor-game. When I looked at his footnotes, it was clear he saw it as a science. And it was clear that he saw it as a species of “game theory.” I’ve seen some confirmatory evidence in the Grove Press archives that suggest it wasn’t just Berne who saw it that way. I’m hoping to work it into this paper.

Berne’s collection of interlocutors for “game analysis” was an interesting collection of people, listed in the footnotes for his theoretical chapter: Stephen Potter’s book on Gamesmanship (a book I always thought of as a piece of popular humor writing), George Herbert Mead (a serious philosopher), and Thomas Szasz (a name that was altogether new to me). Berne also mentioned The San Francisco Social Psychiatry Seminar, which remains an intriguing institution to me. The Szasz citation was the most provocative. His book was called The Myth of Mental Illness, which seemed like an echo of my graduate-school reading of Foucault. Only I noticed that Szasz’s book appeared in 1961, the same year Foucault published Folie et déraison, a tantalizing coincidence.

But what made Szasz interesting for me, at the time, was how much he was involved in the relationship between psychiatry and the courts. Learning as much as I could about Szasz during the same months that I was spending one evening per week in jail alongside a psychiatric social worker made me aware of the relationship between mental health systems and the application of the law. It made Szasz more sympathetic to me, for better or for worse. It certainly helped me see the scope of the problem he was writing about, and its stakes.

item.title: Just another day at the office
item.description:
I want to write a little bit about the genesis of this project, mostly so that I don’t forget. It may also be useful to some reader to peek behind the curtain of how professors at liberal arts colleges work.

Part of where this project came from was a random blog post that I was reading about Murray Edelman, whose concept of “symbolic reassurance” is one of the most powerful and under-examined concepts in the discipline. I find that it’s even more powerful when considered in his own historical context. I’m liable to get bogged down if I write any more about Edelman, so I’ll try to get to the point. It’s going to take a second.

At the time, I was working in an administrative role at the college and didn’t have time to dedicate to serious scholarship. My curiosity was rather untethered and I indulged it in spare moments between trying to establish a program in “public philosophy” and implementation of an expanded, branded “experiential learning” initiative.

So, when I had time to read a blog post on Murray Edelman, I found stray references to an unknown-to-me author named Eric Berne and his book Games People Play. The post didn’t provide a satisfactory explanation of the connection between Berne and Edelman. And so the reference was like a fly to a brook trout: a hook in a swiftly moving stream.

Over the next few months, I put the pieces together of who Berne was: a Canadian who had trained in psychoanalysis and settled in Northern California. It didn’t take much: he’s reasonably well-documented online. He was mostly in private practice, not institutional. But he was well-known in his field as the founder of a therapeutic methodology called “transactional analysis.” Games People Play was a mature expression of this methodology. The book itself, I would learn, is a strange text: part textbook for therapists, part self-help, and partly a book for the general reader. It seemed self-conscious and like it was attempting humor, though most of what he seems to try and pass off as humor are bald-faced misogyny and homophobia. In that regard, parts of it are hard to get through.

In writing my paper on John Dewey I had come across the vocational guidance literature, so I had a basic mental model of how to understand Games People Play, but not one large enough to shake my curiosity off of it.

That’s where the project got its start: a random blog post on an afternoon between administrative tasks.

But I forgot to mention one thing: Games People Play wasn’t some obscure text from the 1960s. It had been a smash for its publisher. It was well-known enough that in 1968 Joe South released a song called “Games People Play,” which won the Grammy for Song of the Year. I’m pretty certain, though I haven’t been able to find the documentary connection that I would need to make the claim in academic writing, that South’s song is inspired by the book and its popularity. The Grove Press archives may have just what I’m after; a publisher like Grove would want their piece of the pie.

It has been recorded by something like two hundred artists since. King Curtis’s instrumental version (Duane Allman on guitar) won a Grammy of its own. Dolly Parton did a version. My favorite is Lee Dorsey’s, on Yes We Can (1970), produced by the inimitable Allen Toussaint.

As unsexy as that sounds, it’s how the project got started. Sometimes the life of the mind is just another day at the office.
